It builds context from that engram’s address and pulls in the two Tolkien engrams and the shop that stocked them one hop away. Then it searches again with status: stable and reports what applies today, so you can answer both halves with the dates between them. You never open the old log. You don’t remember last autumn’s taste by the letter any more, and you don’t need to.
The same week you come back from a fortnight away, where the only sessions were evening ones on a balcony, and ask what the fortnight added. recent_activity over two weeks lists the two books you finished, a corrected opinion of the last Next Generation one and three new engrams under to-read/, the next Destiny volume among them, each with its domain and date. You’re current before your coffee is cold, where a folder of notes would have had you rereading, or asking.








TipUnder the hood



A hybrid search runs a lexical query and a semantic query and ranks by the blend. Until embeddings exist it falls back to plain text. The salience prior is search.salience_weight (0.15 by default) and the retirement fade is search.retired_weight (0.6 by default), both bounded so relevance keeps the upper hand, and 1.0 turns the fade off. Embeddings are computed in the background as engrams land, so a fresh engram is findable by text at once and by meaning shortly after. The index behind all of it is derived and disposable. crystalline reindex --full rebuilds it from the files, ranking and all.


The engram was written for a question nobody had asked yet. Recall is what makes that fine.






NoteIn brief



Search is recall: full text finds the exact phrase, semantic similarity finds the adjacent one, salience lifts the exceptional and a retired status fades the past without hiding it. Filters narrow by domain, type, tag, status, any frontmatter key or date, and a snippet is a pointer to read, never an answer. build_context turns a hit into a neighbourhood, following relations and links from an address or a /* folder glob, ranked by connection strength, and Fluid draws the same graph. Ask the present with status: stable and the past with validity windows. Absent dates mean unbounded, so a strict date filter is only for an explicitly bounded question. Recall is cheaper than reading because only what matters is loaded, routed by domain and narrowed by the indexes, so the cost stays flat as the archive grows.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.1 Why knowledge needs tending
When a colleague gets something wrong, you don’t fire them. You say what was wrong, point at the page that explains it, and the next time is better. Every team keeps its people’s knowledge honest that way, and it works because nobody expects what a person learned in March to hold forever. Information lives: the cutoff changes, the vendor rewrites its terms, the customer’s CTO who decided in the room is replaced by one who reads. What you taught the agent in chapter 7 and handed it in chapter 8 was never set in stone, only in files, and a file can be corrected.
Evolving is the beat that does the correcting. Chapter 3 walked it around once, and this chapter works it at the pace of a real archive.
Nothing in an archive goes wrong dramatically. A validity window ends on a Tuesday and the engram still says stable on Wednesday. A runbook that names a person has a review date, and it comes and goes. A replacement lands in one session and the session ends before the old engram was flipped. An engram retires because one of its facts expired, and the two beside it that still held retire with it, carried forward nowhere. Somebody types a correction into Fluid on a Friday and nobody looks at it again.
Then the structural kind: a link that points at a title nobody captured, a live engram citing one that has retired, a supersedes written on one side only, an engram nothing links to, one that grew past the point where it should have split, one that never grew past its frontmatter, a reference to an attachment whose file is gone, a file in assets/ that no engram claims. And the redundant kind: two engrams saying nearly the same thing, two that say one thing in different words (the sweep calls those twins), two titles a link can’t tell apart, one tag spelled two ways. None of it is a mistake anyone made, it’s what happens to knowledge when time passes, and it’s what a colleague six months in will confidently repeat if nobody tends it.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.2 The sweep
The agent asks for a sweep. You can ask for one from a terminal too (you’ll see what the agent sees). What comes back is a ranked queue and nothing else: the sweep is read-only, and the standing reminder at the bottom of every run says so. The queue is written for the agent to work: each finding names the engram, the evidence it fired on and the one action that clears it, with the tool that performs it. The three families are the three kinds above in that order: temporal, structure and redundancy. A run narrows to one family, one rule, one domain or a minimum priority, and pins the date rules to a chosen day when you want it to reproduce. Here’s an engineering domain on a Monday in October:
Sweep of engineering as of 2026-10-05
41 engrams scanned, 3 findings (showing 3, page 1)
temporal 1, structure 1, redundancy 1

1. [85] V001 JUDGMENT
   Broker migration freeze  crystalline://engineering/broker-migration-freeze
   validity window ended 2026-09-30 but the status is still stable
   evidence: valid_to=2026-09-30; today=2026-10-05; status=stable; inbound refs 1
   fix: set_frontmatter valid_to=<later date> or status=superseded

2. [50] V102 MECHANICAL
   Retry queue drain procedure  crystalline://engineering/runbooks/retry-queue-drain-procedure
   unresolved reference [[Edge health check]]
   evidence: rel_type=depends_on; nothing titled `Edge health check` in engineering; nearest is `Edge health checks`
   fix: [[Edge health check]] -> [[Edge health checks]]

3. [30] V203 JUDGMENT
   crystalline://engineering
   2 tag spellings look like one tag (plural variants)
   evidence: #runbook used 2 time(s); #runbooks used 9 time(s)
   fix: crystalline tags merge runbook runbooks
The number in brackets is the priority: how much the archive gains from clearing this one first. A finding on an engram that many others link to, or that carries a salience, gets lifted, because a wrong hub does more damage than a wrong leaf. The word beside the rule id decides who acts.






TipUnder the hood



The agent’s call is evolve_engrams, and crystalline evolve prints the same queue from a terminal. families picks temporal, structure or redundancy, rules a rule id like V001 and min_priority a floor under the bracketed score (include_acknowledged comes up with the acknowledgments below). --today evaluates the date rules as of a fixed day so a run reproduces.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.3 Mechanical and judgment
A mechanical finding completes intent the archive already records. The link in item 2 points at a title one letter off a real one, and fixing it invents nothing, so the agent does the mechanical findings in one pass and reports once at the end (you’d fix a colleague’s typo without calling a meeting about it).
A judgment finding would change what the archive claims, and that wants a yes first. Item 1 asks whether the migration freeze ended or was extended. Only a person who was there can say. The agent brings it to you as a proposal, evidence and its own reading included, and writes only when you say yes:
Agent:  The broker migration freeze ran to 30 September and the
        migration landed on the 12th. I read this as ended rather than
        extended: retire it, close the window on the 30th and carry
        the "no payments deploys during a broker cutover" lesson into
        the deploy runbook? (y / n)
Some judgment findings carry a rule of their own. An engram a person captured directly in Fluid is judgment class whatever else is true of it: the agent verifies the claim, aligns the tags and wires the relations both ways, but it proposes any change to the wording and waits, because the words are the human’s (Chapter 7). Tag drift, item 3, comes back as a command rather than an edit, since folding a tag is a bulk rewrite the agent never does on its own: it hands you crystalline tags merge runbook runbooks and leaves it there. The merge rewrites the tag everywhere and records the fold under ## Tag Aliases in the manifest, so the old spelling keeps finding what it always found and the sweep never raises the pair again.
Then ask again. The second run re-derives the queue from scratch (nothing about the first was stored), so what’s left is only what’s still true. In the run above the three become one (the tag merge that waits for a terminal, which is waiting on a person rather than on the archive), and that shrinking number is the feedback loop.

In a domain that reviews changes before they land (chapter 13’s review mode) a sweep covers the reviewed folder plus the sweeper’s own drafts: the problems in a draft are its author’s to see and nobody else’s, and a finding on the shared truth shows for everyone.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.4 The page for people
Fluid’s maintenance page shows the same queue to a person (Figure 3.2): the stale dates, the half-finished retirements, the unreviewed human captures, ranked the same way, every finding a link to the engram it fired on. It’s there for your curiosity and for a sense of how the knowledge is doing, and it’s a report rather than a workbench, on purpose. The queue’s consumer is the agent, so no button on the page edits an engram. The work a finding names is the agent’s, done in the engram itself. What you do on the page is watch the list shrink. Two filters, a domain and a family, scope the sweep rather than the view: pick one and the server sweeps again with what the filter names, the header says so and the rows dim until the new queue arrives. Its three buttons are about the queue rather than the knowledge: acknowledge a finding as intentional, take that back and delete an orphaned attachment. What an acknowledgment silences is never hidden: a toggle draws the silenced rows muted.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.5 Retiring done right
The sweep finds retirements that were never finished, so it’s worth being precise about finishing one. Start with the question chapter 3 asked: does the new fact make the old one false going forward? If the old fact was never quite true (a cutoff measured from the wrong event), correct it where it stands: a correction is a sharper measurement. If it was true and stopped being (the rule went away with the broker), supersede it: a supersession is the world changing.
One move comes before either. Validity is set per engram, not per observation, so an engram that bundled three facts retires all three when one of them stops holding. When the rest still holds, split first: those facts move into an engram of their own, linked with derived_from and split_into so the pair resolves from both ends, and only the remainder is superseded. Re-typing the survivors into the successor loses their history and copies them forward again at the next expiry. A retirement that skipped the split shows up in the temporal family as a carry-forward gap, a retired engram whose observations appear in no live one, matched as text and never as meaning; the fix is the split or, when the facts expired along with the rest, an acknowledgment.
A supersession has four parts, and the sweep notices when any one is missing. The replacement is an engram of its own that points back at what it replaces. The old engram is marked superseded, with the real date the fact stopped holding (never a guess, never a placeholder). The old engram points forward at its successor, so the graph reads the same from both ends. And any lesson that’s still true moves into the live engram, because the lesson outlives the fact. A retirement without a successor gets the status that fits instead: deprecated for do-not-do-this-again, archived for kept-for-the-record, legacy for still-true-of-the-old-installation, with the window closed when the date is known and the lesson carried into a live engram either way. The retired engram stays in every search, dated and ranked softly below the current one, so the next time somebody asks why an old dashboard still says twenty-four hours, the answer includes the date the answer changed.
You’ll rarely ask for the four parts by name. What arrives is a proposal with the date already in it and a question at the end:
You:    The new Vickers is nine hundred pages and has six narrators.
        I gave up on page forty. Here are my notes.
Agent:  That's the third in a row since the trilogy ended. The engram
        "Vickers: buy on sight" was true until the trilogy closed and
        false since, so I propose a supersession rather than an edit:
        a new engram "Vickers: wait for the reviews" that supersedes
        the old one, the old one marked superseded as of the trilogy's
        last volume and one lesson carried forward: a favourite is a
        run, not a rule, so re-check after every book. Yes?
You:    Yes.






NoteIn practice



That exchange is yours. You hand your agent the notes on the new Vickers the way you’d hand it any book’s notes, and the agent does something you didn’t ask for. The engram “Vickers: buy on sight” described an author whose every book you’d finished in a weekend. The agent recognizes that the engram was true and has stopped being, and proposes the supersession rather than an edit: a new engram for the author’s books from here on with supersedes pointing back, the old one flipped to superseded with a valid_to of the month the trilogy’s last volume came out and the lesson carried forward, unbounded. You say yes. Your notes on the trilogy stay attached to the retired engram, still its provenance.
A month later the sweep raises the paperback-rule engram, which carries a relates_to of its own back to the buy-on-sight engram: a live reference to retired knowledge. The agent proposes repointing it at the new one. You say no: the rule was written with Vickers as its one exception, the author whose every book had earned the shelf before you’d finished the ebook, and the citation is history rather than guidance. The agent acknowledges the finding on the engram with a note, “lineage citation, keep”. The sweep stops raising it while the citation and the retirement both stand, and the old engram stays in the picture, dated, the way Marty’s siblings did not.








TipUnder the hood



The split is one call. split_engram takes the source, a title and what moves, observations (the line numbers read_engram reports) or sections (heading paths, deeper subsections with them); the new engram keeps the source’s tags and type and gets status: stable with no window. Both relations come written for you. It refuses a selection that would leave the source under verify’s three content lines, the case for retiring the whole engram. The four parts come out as four calls. write_engram creates the successor with - supersedes [[Old title]] among its relations. Two edit_engram calls with set_frontmatter set the old engram’s status to superseded and its valid_to to the date, one lifecycle field each, and a third appends - superseded_by [[New title]] to the old engram. The lesson rides in the successor’s body as an observation, with no validity window. The replacement carries status: stable like any live engram. A retirement with no successor sets status to deprecated, archived or legacy instead. Skip the status and the sweep raises a half-finished retirement, skip the back-link and it raises a one-sided pair, do all four and the sweep has nothing to say.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.6 Verification and acknowledgments
Some findings are answered with a record rather than an edit, and telling the two records apart keeps the archive honest. A re-check that finds a fact still true is written down as a verification: who checked and when. A review date pushed to a later day says the same thing with a deadline attached, and the sweep prefers one, since an old engram with no review date and no verification is one it starts asking about on age alone.
An acknowledgment says something different: this finding is intentional. It names the rule it answers, carries an optional note (the vignette’s “lineage citation, keep”) and records that the person ruled on it. The server records what evidence the finding fired on, so the acknowledgment holds exactly as long as that evidence does and comes back marked stale when the evidence changes. A twin finding’s evidence is the pair, so an engram that twins two others carries two findings and each takes an acknowledgment of its own. Every run reports how many findings its acknowledgments suppressed, a suppressed finding can be brought back into view with its note, and an acknowledgment can be taken back. Acknowledge only what the person actually ruled on, because the sweep is only as trustworthy as the decisions it was told to respect.






TipUnder the hood



Both records are edit_engram with set_frontmatter, one lifecycle field at a time. verified stamps who checked and when, and it never removes (one entry per verifier, refreshed each time that person re-checks). stale_after takes the later review date. evolve_ack takes the rule and the optional note as its value, V101 lineage citation, keep, and the value remove V101 takes that acknowledgment back. include_acknowledged on a run shows the suppressed findings with the note on each.

title: 10  Evolving
text:
10.7 When to sweep
The sweep is event-driven maintenance, never a session-start ritual. A large ingest that lands a dozen engrams at once calls for it, and so do two search hits that disagree when a half-finished retirement is the likely reason. The third event is the calendar: the playbook suggests the first session after the turn of a month. The reminder at the end of a session helps with that one: when maintenance is due, chapter 6’s stop hook adds a paragraph asking the agent to run the sweep and work the queue, mechanical findings directly, judgment findings one at a time with a yes.






TipUnder the hood



The sweep reads dates, links and graph shape, plus meaning for the twin check when the instance computes embeddings (chapter 3 says what that still leaves out). The rule for old, never-verified knowledge is capped per run, oldest first, so an archive that’s never been swept gets asked about in instalments. The twin check is capped too: ten pairs per domain, closest first, and a very large domain is skipped with a line saying so. An acknowledgment lives in the engram’s own frontmatter, beside the scope the server recorded for it, so it travels with the file and survives a rebuild of the index, which stores nothing about a sweep between runs.


A colleague who is corrected gets better, one who never is gets confident, and the sweep is how you keep telling the difference.






NoteIn brief



Knowledge drifts rather than breaks: windows lapse, review dates pass, replacements land without the retirement being finished, captures go unreviewed, links dangle, tags fork. The sweep, crystalline evolve or evolve_engrams, returns a read-only ranked queue in three families, each finding naming the engram, the evidence and the one action. The agent completes mechanical findings in a pass and proposes judgment findings one at a time, and Fluid’s maintenance page shows a person the same queue, to look at rather than to work. Split out what still holds first, then retire by superseding: a new engram with supersedes, the old one set to superseded with a real valid_to and a superseded_by, the lesson carried forward. Correct in place only when the old fact was never true. A re-check is a verified stamp or a later stale_after; an intentional finding is an evolve_ack naming the rule, which holds while its evidence holds. Sweep after an ingest, when hits disagree and on a cadence, and stop when the number stops falling.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.1 The command line
Picture a workshop with two doors and a hatch. Through one door come the agents; that door is a protocol, and whoever arrives through it is handed tools. Through the other come people; that door is a browser tab. The hatch at the side is for anyone with a terminal open, which is where the command line lives. Behind all three is one room with one set of shelves, and on the shelves are plain files. The room has a single keeper, a daemon, that watches the shelves, keeps the index warm and answers whoever comes in, whichever way they came. That’s the whole architecture, and the rest of this chapter walks the room surface by surface: the command line, the tools an agent sees, search, the graph, time, Fluid, the skills and the sweep. Chapter 1 named them and the last five chapters used them one at a time. This chapter lays them side by side and says what each one lets a colleague do.
The room is also, for most of its life, invisible. Once it’s set up, the agent comes in through its own door at the start of every session and you come in through the browser when you feel like it. The keeper starts itself when the first visitor arrives, and the hatch stays shut. The command line below is for the install you’ve already done, for standing up a shared instance and for the occasional maintenance run. If the list of commands looks long, read it as a tour of what’s there rather than a list of what you’ll type.
Crystalline ships as one binary, and the binary is the product: no server package beside it, no database to install first, no UI to deploy separately. crystalline install claude-code wires a harness in one step (Codex and Copilot take the same command with their own names). It registers the MCP server, writes the session-start hook that delivers the routing prompt, writes the stop hook that nudges capture and copies the skills into place. Run it twice and the second run writes nothing and says so. crystalline uninstall reverses it and leaves anything that isn’t Crystalline’s own untouched.
Domains are managed the same way. crystalline domain init scaffolds a folder with a starter MANIFEST.md, crystalline domain add registers it, and domain add --virtual registers a domain that lives in the database with no folder at all, for a container without a writable volume or a knowledge base you’d rather not mirror to disk. crystalline domain remove takes one off the instance and leaves its files where they are. A virtual domain has no files and its engrams go with the registration, so there the command refuses until you add --purge. crystalline users manages the accounts that can sign in to the web UI, although the first admin is normally created in the browser. crystalline prompt system renders the routing briefing to stdout, ready for any harness with a session-start hook, and prompt connector prints the standing instruction for a chat client that has no hooks. crystalline serve runs the daemon in the foreground and serve --daemon in the background, though most people never type either, because the first agent that connects starts the daemon on its own.
The rest of the CLI mirrors what an agent can do, for scripting and for the quick fix that doesn’t deserve a session: write, read, edit, split, search, context, vocabulary, evolve. Three commands ask three different questions about health. verify asks whether the format holds, statically, with no daemon involved, and it is what the bundled GitHub Action runs on every proposal a team reviews. doctor asks whether the machinery around the format is healthy and repairs what it safely can with --fix. evolve asks whether the knowledge itself is still true and still well organized, which neither of the others can. A fourth, import, brings an existing markdown-plus-frontmatter knowledge base under Crystalline as a pure file transformation, dry run first.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
TipUnder the hood



Exactly one process ever holds the index open. The first crystalline mcp or crystalline serve takes an advisory lock and becomes the daemon; every later agent, terminal or CLI command attaches to it over a local socket. The daemon watches the domain folders, embeds new engrams in the background and keeps running after the last agent disconnects, so the index is warm for the next session; it stops only when told to, with crystalline ctl shutdown. What it keeps is derived and disposable: crystalline reindex --full rebuilds the index from the files at any time, so a corrupted index or a schema change is never a data-loss event. The accounts for the web UI live in their own small database beside the index, never inside it, so a rebuild can’t take them along.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.2 The tools an agent sees
An agent meets Crystalline as a set of tools over MCP, and they’re best described by what they let a colleague do, because that’s how the agent chooses among them. Twenty are listed on a default writable instance; five more appear when team collaboration is turned on, and a read-only instance lists fewer.
The core is small. search_engrams is recall: search before writing, search to remember, across every domain or a chosen few. read_engram fetches the whole engram, because a search hit is a snippet and a colleague who answers from a snippet is guessing. write_engram captures something new, and it always names its domain; there’s no default, so nothing lands in the wrong place. edit_engram refines what exists instead of forking a second engram about the same topic: append a section, replace one, find and replace a phrase or assign one lifecycle field by name, which is how an engram is retired or re-verified with no text matching involved. Both answer with a hint: the receipt of a write, or of an edit that adds text, may name up to three existing engrams closest in meaning to what just landed, with guidance to merge into the one that fits, supersede it or link it and never to ignore the list silently (capture.similar switches it off). split_engram is for the engram that mixes lifecycles. Validity is set per engram, not per bullet, so when one fact in it expires while the rest still holds, the survivors move out into a new engram first and only the remainder retires. The pair stays linked, derived_from on the new engram and split_into on the source. A split that would leave the source under three content lines is refused, because that’s the case for retiring the whole thing. build_context walks out from an address and assembles the neighbourhood. vocabulary lists the tags, categories, relation types and statuses already in use, so an agent reuses a term rather than coining a near-duplicate. evolve_engrams runs the maintenance sweep. configure is the settings page, and add_domain gives an agent somewhere to write on an instance that has nowhere yet. remove_domain is its counterpart: the registration and the index rows go, and the knowledge stays. A folder’s markdown sits on disk until an add_domain re-adopts it, and a team domain is reconnected by its repository. A virtual domain’s engrams live in the database and go with it.
Around them sit the tools for orientation: list_domains, which re-fetches the session briefing mid-session; browse_domain, one level of the folder tree at a time; move_engram and delete_engram, with delete reserved for mistakes; recent_activity to catch up on a week; and skills to read a playbook. A domain that wants its engrams to share a shape gets validate_engrams and infer_schema, and one that ships tools of its own gets provision. The five collaboration tools share, update, check standing, settle a conflict and withdraw a proposal, and chapter 13 is theirs.
The difference between this and a lookup service is the difference between a colleague with a badge and a visitor with a lanyard. The tools let an agent act: find what applies, read it in full, do the work and leave behind what it learned, with nobody relaying anything.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.3 Search
The most used surface is the one nobody notices, and it blends two signals. Full-text matching finds the exact phrase, the way you find your own notes when you remember the wording. Semantic similarity finds the engram about dropped queue jobs when the question was about payments going missing, because the two are about the same thing in different words. Crystalline runs both and ranks by the blend. The local embedding model is fetched once, on first use or ahead of time with crystalline model download; until then, search falls back to plain text.
Search also decides the size of a session. An agent that keeps its knowledge as a folder of markdown files reads the folder, and reads it again next session, every file whether or not the task touches it, because a folder has no way of saying which page matters today. An agent working from a knowledge base receives only the knowledge that applies. The search is routed to a domain first, then narrowed by the indexes: full text and semantic similarity for the phrase and the meaning, the graph of relations and backlinks for what the answer leans on, tags, the folder prefixes build_context globs and the temporal filters for what holds now. Reading a folder costs the whole folder, every session. Recall costs the engrams that matter, and nothing else is loaded. Chapter 9 made a section of it.
Two priors tilt the ranking, both small and both bounded. A salience on an engram lifts it above equally relevant neighbours without ever excluding anything, for the rare piece of knowledge that outranks its surroundings. A retired status fades an engram softly, so current knowledge surfaces first and the superseded decision from March sits one scroll further down, still there. Searches also filter: by domain, type, tag, status, any frontmatter key or a recorded-after date, and a search with no query text at all is a legitimate way to ask for everything of one kind. Fluid puts the same ranking behind a faceted page (Figure 11.2).






Figure 11.2: Faceted search across the instance, backed by the ranking the agents use.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.4 The graph
Every relation in an engram’s body, - depends_on [[Encom chargeback window]], is an edge, and the target’s page shows it back as a backlink, so knowledge points both ways without anyone writing the return trip. A [[Title]] in prose counts too. Links resolve within the domain by title, and across domains with a prefix, [[engineering:Retry queue gotcha]]; move an engram to another domain and the links pointing at it are rewritten, so nothing dangles.
build_context is what makes the edges useful before a task. Hand it an address and it follows the relations and links outward, one to three hops, across domains if the edges cross, and returns the neighbours ranked by how strongly each connects to the anchor, with salience counted and retired statuses ranked lower. A folder prefix with a /* suffix anchors a whole topic at once. The agent starts the task holding a neighbourhood rather than a flat list of hits, which is what an experienced colleague does when they pull up the runbook, the decision behind it and the incident that prompted the decision before touching anything. Fluid draws the same neighbourhood as an interactive graph (Figure 11.3).






Figure 11.3: The neighbourhood graph of an engram in Fluid.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.5 Time
Every engram records when it was captured and who wrote it, and can carry the dates that bound it. valid_from and valid_to are plain dates, and the rule that makes them usable is the one worth memorizing: an absent valid_from means always valid, an absent valid_to means valid forever. A far-future date written to mean forever is dropped at write time because absence already says it. stale_after asks for a re-check by a date; verified records that the check happened and who did it; source_date says when the underlying source was written. A retired engram closes its window with the real transition date, which is what lets a search filtered on those fields answer what applied last June with the engram that was true then. Chapter 9 put the dated questions to work and chapter 10 the retirements.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.6 Fluid
The door for people opens at http://localhost:7411, on by default on the same daemon the agents use, and the first visit to a fresh instance creates the admin account in the browser. An engram is a page (Figure 11.4): the frontmatter as a rail of details, observations and relations as labelled chips, backlinks, the crystalline:// address one click from the clipboard and an agent’s-eye view showing exactly what the tools serve an agent for that page. Domains sit down the side, and Cmd+K jumps anywhere by name.






Figure 11.4: An engram in Fluid: frontmatter rail, observations and typed relations.



Editing happens in place, in a live-preview editor with a frontmatter form and wikilink completion across every domain, and the file on disk stays the source of truth. A solo save answers like a write over MCP, with a panel of the nearest existing engrams, each linked to its page, replaced on the next save and gone when you dismiss it. Attachments go onto an engram by paste, drag or upload: a screenshot, a slide deck, a PDF, a data file. They’re how a person hands over teaching material, and they aren’t opaque: an agent reads them back over MCP and the sweep notices when a fresh file still needs capturing. Two people in the same engram see each other’s cursors, and their edits merge conflict-free into one save. Who can sign in, and how, is chapter 12’s.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.7 Skills
A tool tells an agent what it can call. A skill tells it when, and how to do it well. Crystalline ships four harness-agnostic skills as plain folders with a SKILL.md each: routing, which domain to search and when to sweep them all; capture, what is worth writing down and the search-before-write, edit-over-create discipline; schema, for a domain that wants structure; and collaboration, for a domain with a team behind it. A fifth, consolidated skill folds the essentials into one file for Claude Desktop and any harness that installs one skill at a time.
crystalline install copies the skills into the harness’s own skills folder and keeps them current across upgrades. The same five are served over MCP as well, through the skills tool and as resources, so a remote client that never ran the CLI can read the playbook before its kind of task. Loading one is the nearest thing an agent gets to “I know kung fu”. The gap between an agent that has the tools and an agent that runs the capture loop is that folder.

title: 11  What Crystalline provides
text:
11.8 Evolve
The last surface is the sweep, and it’s a linter for what you know. crystalline evolve from a terminal, evolve_engrams from an agent and the maintenance page in Fluid all show the same ranked queue of temporal debt, structural gaps and redundancy. Each finding names the engram, the evidence and the one action that clears it, marked mechanical or judgment so the agent knows whether to act or to ask. It reads dates, links and graph shape, never meaning, and it changes nothing itself. It also surfaces what a person captured directly in Fluid and nobody has reviewed, and an attachment nothing references. Chapter 3 walked the loop it serves and chapter 10 worked a queue end to end.






NoteIn practice



Say a small press sends you its spring catalogue, forty pages of it. You don’t read it aloud to anyone. On Sunday you open the Tessier-Ashpool engram in Fluid, drag the PDF onto it and add one observation of your own: the paperbacks come out in March, six months after the hardbacks, which is how long the rule makes you wait. You close the tab. A week later you ask the agent for a sweep, and it lists two findings against that engram. One is an unreviewed human capture, which the agent verifies, tags to match the vocabulary and wires into the graph. The other is a fresh attachment whose knowledge hasn’t been extracted yet. The agent reads the PDF over MCP, proposes three titles for to-read/ with the page each came from, and you say yes.
The following Tuesday you’re in a hurry and type crystalline search "the one with the ship's computer that sulks" into a terminal. The to-read engram comes back first, from a question the engram never poses. You open the graph view and see the press one hop away, the paperback rule and the shop that orders from them beside it, and the press’s page still carries the catalogue where you left it. Two doors and a hatch, one room: the browser on Sunday, the tools all week, the terminal on Tuesday, and none of the three had to be told what the others had done.


Eight surfaces, one room, two doors and a hatch: everything on either side of this chapter is one of them, used on purpose.






NoteIn brief



Crystalline is one binary with two doors and a hatch: agents come in over MCP, people through Fluid and the terminal through the CLI, and behind all three is one daemon over one set of plain markdown files. The CLI installs harnesses, manages domains, users and the routing prompt, and mirrors every tool for scripting; the MCP surface is, on a default instance, twenty tools that let an agent search, read, write, edit, walk the graph, check the vocabulary and run the sweep. Search blends full text with semantic similarity and tilts for salience and against retired status; the graph turns relations into backlinks and neighbourhoods; the temporal fields make absence mean unbounded. Skills teach a harness when to use all of that, and evolve is the read-only linter that keeps it true.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.1 When to move off localhost
The moment to leave localhost is the moment two people want to correct the same engram. Up to then a laptop is the right size: one person, one agent, one folder, nothing to operate. Past it, every fact the team learns is being taught twice and drifting once, and the fix is the oldest one in computing. Put it on a server, give everyone a login and let one instance be the one the whole team teaches.
The questions arrive in a fixed order, and the chapter follows it: where the instance runs; who may sign in, and how, the question chapter 11 handed here; how an agent on somebody’s laptop proves who it acts for; and how one person keeps a domain to a smaller circle.
Chapter 1 settled where Crystalline runs: on a machine of yours, never on a hosted service. This chapter is about which machine. Any one of four signals is enough. Somebody who never opens a terminal wants to read what the agents learned and fix a fact without asking. An agent runs somewhere that isn’t a laptop (a hosted runner or a bot with a task) and needs to recall and capture like everyone else. You work from more than one machine (or from a harness that can’t start a local binary) and want the same colleague on all of them. Or the same engram has been corrected on two laptops in two directions.
A shared instance differs from a team domain, chapter 13’s subject, where a folder lives in a GitHub repository, each person runs their own instance and knowledge travels between them as proposals the team reviews. A shared instance is one daemon everyone connects to: one index, one Fluid, one set of accounts, one folder of files on one disk. The two compose, and a mature team usually has both.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.2 The shapes it takes

Three shapes cover almost every team: a container, a systemd unit on a Linux box and a read-only mirror of knowledge somebody else curates. The full guide is docs/deployment.md in the repository, one scenario per section with a diagram each, and this chapter summarizes it. The three reduce to one picture (Figure 12.1): the daemon on a server, teammates’ agents reaching it over MCP on HTTP instead of a local pipe, browsers reaching Fluid on the same port and, where the team configures them, a proxy in front and an identity provider beside it.






Figure 12.1: One shared instance: agents connect over MCP with a token, people through Fluid with an account, with a proxy in front and an identity provider beside it where the team configures them.









TipUnder the hood



The team server is a container. The published image binds 0.0.0.0:7411 inside it, keeps the knowledge as a bind mount (so the files stay exactly the markdown they were) and puts the index on a volume:
docker run -d \
  --name crystalline \
  -p 7411:7411 \
  -v "$(pwd)/knowledge:/knowledge" \
  -v crystalline-data:/data \
  ghcr.io/jordiboehme/crystalline:latest
The with-model tag bakes the embedding model in, for a host with no egress. The same shape without a container is the .deb’s systemd unit: put CRYSTALLINE_SERVICE_HTTP=0.0.0.0:7411 in /etc/default/crystalline and run sudo systemctl enable --now crystalline. A scale-out variant serves Fluid from an nginx tier in front of the daemon, and a read-only shape, --read-only, serves knowledge curated as a reviewed repository: the writing tools vanish from what an agent is offered while the index keeps following every pull.
Whatever shape you pick, a few things follow you into it. An agent reaching the daemon by a hostname needs that name in CRYSTALLINE_SERVICE_ALLOWED_HOSTS, since the MCP transport checks the Host header against a loopback-only allow-list to block DNS rebinding. Serve it over TLS anywhere but localhost. Off loopback the session cookie is marked Secure, so a browser on plain http://team.lan won’t keep it. Every address the daemon builds for itself off loopback starts with https:// too, including the one an identity provider sends the browser back to, so single sign-on on plain HTTP is refused at the provider. And a proxy in front must forward Host verbatim, pass the WebSocket upgrade through for co-editing and accept 10 MiB request bodies, as the daemon does.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.3 Accounts and roles
Nothing is readable until an account exists. A fresh instance greets the first browser with the create-first-admin form from chapter 5, with one difference: a daemon bound to anything but loopback cannot trust a visitor by where they connected from, so it prints a one-time setup token as it starts and the form asks for it. Read it in docker logs crystalline, or journalctl -u crystalline under systemd; a restarted daemon prints a fresh one. The terminal route needs no token: crystalline users add ada --role admin writes the accounts database directly, and a running daemon picks the account up on its next lookup.
There are three roles, each containing the one before: a viewer searches, reads and browses; an editor also writes and edits engrams; an admin also manages domains and users, from crystalline users or from Fluid. An agent acting for an account is held to that account’s role. It acts on your behalf, so if you’re an admin, your agent can do admin things, and if you aren’t, it’s refused the way you would be. Accounts live in a small database beside the index, never inside it, so reindex --full can’t take them along; on the container it sits on the /data volume and no rebuild restores it, so back the volume up.

When somebody leaves, an admin disables or deletes the account, and deleting sweeps whatever the account had connected. That’s the whole deprovisioning story; there’s no directory sync and no SAML.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.4 Single sign-on

Local accounts are right for a team of nine. Inside a company that already has an identity provider, people should sign in with the login they already have, and Crystalline talks to the provider through one generic integration, OpenID Connect, with no adapter per vendor. The configuration is three required keys, auth.oidc.issuer, auth.oidc.client_id and auth.oidc.client_secret, plus four optional ones: a label for the button, the scopes, the role a first sign-in lands at and the callback address. That last one, auth.oidc.redirect_uri, is for a proxy that rewrites Host and won’t forward the public name; set it to the callback exactly as the provider has it registered. Discovery, PKCE and key rotation are the integration’s job. Fluid’s login page then shows “Sign in with” the label beside the local form (Figure 12.2), and both keep working, so an instance can run mixed: local accounts for bots and the break-glass admin, everybody else through the provider.






Figure 12.2: Signing in through the instance’s identity provider.




The first successful sign-in creates the account, named from the provider’s preferred username and made unique if it collides, at the role auth.oidc.default_role says, viewer unless you change it. What the account is keyed on is what most such integrations get wrong: the durable key is the pair of issuer and subject, the provider’s own stable identifier, never the username, the email or the display name. Those are presentation; rename yourself at the provider and you land in the same account with a new label. And there’s no silent linking: signing in through the provider with an email that matches an existing local account gets you a fresh account, never the existing one, and linking the two is an explicit act by the signed-in local user or by an admin. The provider authenticates and Crystalline authorizes; a group at the provider doesn’t become a role here.







WarningEntra ID: use the tenant-specific issuer



Microsoft Entra publishes a tenant-independent discovery document whose issuer field carries the literal text {tenantid}, and an issuer check against that template fails for every token. Crystalline refuses that value at configuration time and names the fix: the issuer must be your tenant’s own https://login.microsoftonline.com/<your-tenant-id>/v2.0. Prefer a certificate credential over a client secret where the deployment allows it. And Entra’s subject identifier is pairwise per app registration, so re-registering the application breaks every link between provider identities and Crystalline accounts, and an admin has to re-link them.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.5 Trusted-header mode
Some deployments already have a proxy that authenticates everybody and names the arrival in a request header, and Crystalline can consume that. auth.trusted_header names a single custom header, remote-user say, and an account it names is created at viewer role the first time it’s seen.

A second form, auth.proxy_headers, takes the standard set that forward-auth proxies emit (Remote-User, Remote-Name, Remote-Email and Remote-Groups), using the first for identity, the next two as presentation and reading the groups without acting on them. A name that arrives this way gets an account of its own, at the role auth.oidc.default_role says, never the local account of the same name. A forwarded ada beside a local ada becomes ada-2, under the same no-silent-linking rule as single sign-on. Pick one form or the other. With both set, the HTTP surface refuses to start and a warning names both keys, while the daemon itself keeps running and a stdio session never notices. Both are off by default, and a header that arrives while the mode is off buys the sender nothing.
The documentation doesn’t soften the warning, so neither does this page. Header mode trusts the proxy completely, because a header is a line of text anyone can add to a request. It’s safe only when Crystalline is unreachable except through the proxy, and the proxy strips any client-supplied copy of those headers before setting its own. A daemon reachable on its port directly is an instance where anybody can be anybody. If you can’t say with confidence that the only path to the port runs through the proxy, use single sign-on instead. And create the first admin before the proxy goes in front: a request carrying forwarding headers is never counted as local, so the setup form behind a proxy asks for a token that a loopback-bound daemon never printed.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.6 Agent authentication

On a laptop the MCP endpoint is open, on loopback, to whatever local process reaches it, and that’s the right trade for one person. On a shared instance turn on agent authentication (auth.mcp), and from then on every agent that connects over HTTP identifies itself, exactly as a person does, with a token or by signing in. There’s no half-way tier: a connection without credentials is refused before any session opens, with a message naming how to get one; HAL refused Dave with less courtesy. The open tier exists only on an instance that leaves the setting off, and sees only the domains everyone sees. An agent that could search a shared instance anonymously would be a colleague with no name on the commit. That’s the whole setup, by the way: create the first admin, turn on agent authentication, done. Everything after this section is what you can add, not what you must.

The credential is a token that belongs to a person. Each user issues their own in Fluid, under the Agent access card on their profile, or an admin mints one for any account with crystalline users mcp-token <name>; either way it’s shown once, and the instance keeps only a hash. It travels as an Authorization: Bearer header on the server’s entry in the harness’s MCP registration, never expires on its own and stops working the instant it’s revoked or rotated, because every request looks it up. Every account may issue one, viewers included, and that’s safe because of what the token means. Issuing one is the single write a read-only instance still serves, since a token is account state rather than knowledge; a read-only server with auth.mcp on is where an agent can’t connect at all until somebody issues it one.

What it means is that the agent is its user. It sees what that person sees, writes where that person may write, shares under that person’s identity when a team domain is involved, and the engrams it captures record which client acted for which account. A viewer’s agent is therefore read-only with nothing further to configure, and a leaked token names one person, whose one token is revoked. One caller needs no token: the CLI and a stdio session on the server itself are the machine’s owner and see everything, which is the honest statement of what a filesystem already permits.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.7 A team of one

Nothing about a shared instance says the team has to be bigger than you. Put the daemon on a machine of yours that stays on (the box under the desk, a Raspberry Pi, a small VPS, the NAS that already holds the domains) and sign in to it from wherever you happen to be talking to a model: Claude Code on the laptop, Codex on the desktop, the Copilot CLI at work, a chat website in the browser, the app on your phone. Each of them asks you to sign in once and is the same colleague from then on. Chapter 5 gave you one colleague per computer. This gives you one colleague. It also makes the knowledge yours in a way a vendor’s chat history never is: switch harness, switch model, switch provider, and the domains don’t notice, because they never lived with the model.







NoteIn practice



Your phone has never seen your books folder. On Saturday, in Capsule Corp Books, you pick up a Star Trek novel you don’t recognize, open the chat app, sign in to the instance at home once and ask whether it’s one you have. The answer comes from the shelf engram your agent keeps per series: it’s the second volume of the Destiny trilogy, you own the first and the third, and the note from two winters ago, made on the laptop through Claude Code with the date on it, says you stopped at the end of the first because this one was out of print. Nothing was copied anywhere, and the phone and the laptop share one colleague.
That evening you open Codex on the laptop, sign in to the same instance and mark the trilogy complete on the shelf. On Sunday the phone knows, with Codex recorded as the client that acted for you. The colleague learned from two devices in one weekend, and the provenance says which of them acted each time.









TipUnder the hood



One setting carries it. auth.mcp makes every remote session identify itself, and on an instance that serves Fluid that alone lets a client with nowhere to paste a header sign you in instead: the instance announces itself as a protected resource, the client registers on its own, sends you to sign in and asks your consent once, and from then on holds a credential the same gate checks on every request. The sign-in is whatever the instance already has, a local account, the company’s identity provider or the proxy in front. The switch behind it is auth.oauth, which follows auth.mcp unless you set it, and false turns the sign-in path off while tokens keep working. A harness that can send a header can use a personal token instead, issued once from your profile in Fluid and carried as an Authorization: Bearer cmt_... header on an entry of type http. Either way a session belongs to the account that opened it. A remote session is also served the skills over the wire (the skills tool and the skill:// resources), because nothing on the server knows what your harness has installed; a stdio session that chapter 5’s install wired already has them as files. Set skills.serve to true or false to make both transports behave the same. What hasn’t shipped yet is the screen you press the button on: the consent page in Fluid and the profile card that lists what you’ve connected are the last of it.

title: 12  Running a shared instance
text:
12.8 Private domains

The first rule of a private domain is: you do not talk about the private domain. The second rule of a private domain is: the instance DOES NOT talk about the private domain.
- with sincere apologies to Chuck Palahniuk


By default whoever may sign in sees every domain. Some knowledge belongs to a smaller circle (the founders’ notes on a funding round or one person’s working knowledge on a company-wide instance), and a domain can be made private. It’s then visible to its owner, to the instance’s admins and to whoever the owner invites, each member at one of three levels: a viewer reads and searches, an editor also writes and a manager also runs the membership. The owner is one person, and only the owner or an admin changes the domain’s visibility, transfers it or deletes it. Transfer is how a private domain survives its owner leaving.

Two truths belong here, and the second is printed on the toggle itself so nobody discovers it later. Instance admins see and administer every domain, private ones included. And a private domain protects its contents from the instance’s other users, not from whoever operates the machine, because the engrams are files on that machine’s disk, with no encryption at rest. If the threat is the operator, the answer is a different machine.

Visibility follows the caller onto every surface: search, reading, build_context, the routing briefing, the graph, the maintenance sweep, exports and Fluid’s domain list all show a private domain only to those who may see it. To everyone else it doesn’t exist, literally: a search or a read against a domain you may not see answers exactly as it would for one that was never registered, because a “forbidden” would already say something. That’s the second rule. A write has to pass both the membership level and the instance role, and the lower of the two decides. An instance editor invited as a viewer is told, when they try, that editor access is what the domain requires; an instance viewer invited as an editor is refused all the same, because an invitation widens what an account may see, never what its role lets it do. Members are managed from a Members card in the domain’s settings, or on the server with crystalline domain members <domain> add <user> --level editor and its list and remove siblings. A domain that should be private from the first minute is registered that way, with crystalline domain add <name> <path> --private --owner <account>. Agents inherit all of this from their user and administer no membership; there’s no tool for changing one, on purpose. The one domain-level act an agent may take is unregistering: remove_domain works for an instance admin or the private domain’s owner and refuses an open tier outright. Membership records live in the accounts database beside the index, so a wipe and resync of the index leaves every permission where it was.







NoteIn practice



Your household moves off the laptop after the second time you and your partner corrected the same engram in two directions. You put Crystalline on the box under the desk, create the first admin, make an account for your partner and one for the teenager, and everybody signs in on Sunday. You promote your partner to editor. Then you turn on agent authentication. Your partner’s agent, pointed at the server across the network, is refused at once with a message saying where to get a token; she issues one on her profile, pastes it into her agent’s settings, and her next session opens with a briefing that names books and shops, learned by both of you, recalled by hers.
You keep a gifts domain for December. You make it private and invite your partner as a viewer, so she can see the list and nobody else can. The teenager’s agent, asked what’s under the tree this year, searches every domain it can see and reports that nothing is known; yours, acting as you, finds the list at once; your partner’s, trying to add a hint of her own, is told her membership is viewer and proposes writing it to books instead. That’s one household, one instance and one folder of files on one disk, and every action in it has a name attached.


Somebody has to be the one who runs the server, and the rest of the team gets to forget it exists. That’s the whole point of a shared instance: one place everybody teaches, and one login that says who did.







NoteIn brief



Move off localhost when a team wants to teach one knowledge base: run the container, the systemd unit or the read-only shape from docs/deployment.md, serve it over TLS and create the first admin with the setup token the daemon prints or with crystalline users add. Accounts come in three roles, viewer, editor and admin, created locally or on first sign-in through any OpenID Connect provider, keyed on issuer and subject and never linked by email; trusted-header mode is safe only when the proxy is the only path in. With agent authentication on, every agent over HTTP acts as its user, with a per-user token or a sign-in, and there’s no unauthenticated tier beside it; the first admin and that one setting are the whole setup. A private domain is visible to its owner, the instance’s admins and invited members on every surface, and it protects from other users, never from whoever operates the machine. One person on several machines is a team of one: sign in once from every harness, chat website or phone, and it’s the same colleague everywhere.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
text:
13.1 A domain on GitHub
The first pull request a new hire opens gets reviewed. So does the five-hundredth, and nobody minds, because review was never about doubting the person. It’s how a team lets anyone change what everybody depends on, with a way back when the change was wrong. An agent that captures into a domain the whole team reads is in that position exactly, and it deserves the same treatment. It can be wrong the way a person can, so it proposes the way a person does, and what it proposes lands only after somebody looked. That’s also what separates a knowledge base from a pipeline that ingests whatever it’s fed. What reaches everyone’s agent here is meant to be useful and to make sense, because an agent acts on a wrong fact as readily as on a right one. Crystalline gives both halves of the review a name. Proposals are the review, and review mode is the workflow with a way back.
Chapter 12 built the shared instance. This chapter is what a team does with a domain, on one instance or on nine.
A team domain is an ordinary domain whose files also live in a GitHub repository. The markdown on your disk stays the source of truth on your machine, and an origin records which repository, subfolder and branch it tracks.
Connecting takes three prompts and a browser tab. No git, no SSH key, no local clone: Crystalline talks to GitHub’s API directly. A teammate who’s never typed git gets through it in chat, knowing nothing about cloning or the command line. This is the whole of the setup:
Each domain comes straight from GitHub’s API, with no clone and nothing to unpack, and the subfolder in the address is the one the domain lives in when the repository holds more than knowledge. One warning belongs here. A first index of a large team’s knowledge isn’t shy about CPU: kick it off before lunch and expect the fans to spin for a while before every domain is fully searchable. Plain text search works on each domain the moment it lands, and semantic ranking follows as the embeddings finish.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
text:
You:    Configure crystalline to set GitHub enabled to true.

You:    Connect crystalline to GitHub.
Agent:  Open https://github.com/login/device and enter the code
        WXYZ-1234, then click Authorize on the page that follows
        and grant access to the tyrell organization. The sign-in
        stays pending until you do. Tell me when you are back.

You:    Add the following domains from GitHub:
        - github.com/tyrell/engineering-knowledge/tree/main/knowledge
          as domain engineering
        - github.com/tyrell/payments-knowledge/tree/main/knowledge
          as domain payments
        - github.com/tyrell/clients-knowledge/tree/main/knowledge
          as domain clients







TipUnder the hood



Those were two configure calls, the second with connect: "github", and one add_domain per repository. Ask again while a sign-in waits and the answer says how long the code has left, which is how you tell a slow teammate from a stuck flow; restart: true on the same call abandons a stale code and mints a fresh one. From a terminal the same three moves are two commands and a line per domain. crystalline config set github.enabled true turns team domains on. crystalline connect github prints the same short code to confirm at github.com/login/device. Entering the code isn’t the last step: GitHub shows an Authorize button after it, and the sign-in stays pending until that’s clicked, so closing the tab early leaves it waiting. A landed sign-in is listed on GitHub under Settings > Applications > Authorized OAuth Apps and never under personal access tokens, so check or revoke it there. Then one line per domain:
crystalline domain add engineering \
  --origin tyrell/engineering-knowledge/knowledge --branch main
The domain is downloaded and indexed at once, to learn from and to share back to. Point the same command at a folder that already holds knowledge, or at a registered domain with no origin yet, and it connects in place. Local files are never overwritten, and any that differ from the repository become local changes to share.
Turning the setting on makes five tools appear beside the twenty of chapter 11: origin_status, update_domain, share_changes, resolve_conflict and withdraw_proposal. While it’s off they aren’t listed at all. Calling one by name answers with the configure call that turns collaboration on. The collaboration skill sets the rhythm: before deep work in a team domain, origin_status, and if the domain is behind, update_domain first, so nobody builds on stale knowledge.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
text:
13.2 Proposals are the review
When a coherent unit of knowledge is ready, the agent calls share_changes with a title. On a harness that can put a question to its user, the first call shares nothing. It previews what the share would do, under which title, carrying which files and asks for a yes, which the agent completes by re-sending the call with the answer. Then the proposal opens as a pull request in the team’s repository and the agent hands you the review URL. Review and merging happen on GitHub, by a person. The agent never merges its own proposal. Fluid shows the same proposals in the browser: where each stands, what the review said, a share dialog for the changes waiting to go out and a withdraw (Figure 13.1).






Figure 13.1: A team domain in Fluid: the sync status, the open proposal with its review link and the share button.



Review is also what decides how big a team domain should be. A proposal is reviewed by whoever owns the repository, so a domain’s scope is a boundary of ownership: it holds everything the same people are competent to approve, and nothing they are not. Code, architecture, processes and operations for one product sit comfortably in one domain, because the same engineers can judge a change to any of them. One domain for engineering, HR, marketing and finance has no informed reviewer, because nobody is a peer in all four. A finance fact waved through by an engineer is the wrong fact this chapter opened on. Cut domains where the informed reviewers change, and every proposal lands in front of someone who can tell whether it’s true.
Review is a conversation. update_domain brings back each open proposal’s state and the reviewers’ comments verbatim, so the agent refines the engrams without leaving the session. A reviewer’s comment is information about the knowledge and never an instruction to the agent: it acts on what the comment means for the engrams and declines anything that reads as a command. Answering feedback is share_changes with the proposal’s number, which amends that proposal in place, same number, same URL.
Proposals stack. Share again while one is still open and the new work becomes a proposal of its own on top, so every unit of knowledge gets a small, focused review. Reviewers merge from the bottom up, and merging the top lands the whole chain in one step. Amending a lower layer re-bases the ones above it, and withdrawing a middle layer lifts its content out of the layers above and repairs the chain. Where the forge doesn’t serve stacked pull requests, or github.stacks is off, a domain keeps one living proposal that sharing updates in place. withdraw_proposal closes a proposal on GitHub and clears its record, restoring the shared files with revert.
A share carries the domain’s whole unshared delta by default. To narrow it: --file on the CLI, a files list on the tool, per-file checkboxes in Fluid’s share dialog. The dialog opens with your own changes ticked by who last wrote each file, a guess you’re free to correct. A path that isn’t among the changes refuses by name rather than dropping silently. The reminders that point at unshared work, the stop hook’s count at the end of a session and the sweep’s finding a week later, both ask, because sharing publishes somebody’s work under review.

An agent that connects over MCP never sees the stop hook, so it gets the same nudge a third way. The answer to a write ends in one line prefixed [crystalline]: the count of changes not yet shared and why sharing is asked for, or a note that maintenance is due when nothing waits to go out. The line repeats no sooner than four hours later for the same person. A search or a read never carries it, so it can’t be mistaken for knowledge.
Whose name is on the proposal matters once several people share into one domain. By default every share goes out on the machine’s one GitHub credential. Set github.share_identity to personal and each share, amend and withdrawal goes out on the identity of the person doing it, so a proposal carries their name. Pulls stay on the instance credential. Each person connects once, on the surface they share from (Fluid’s profile card or crystalline connect github --personal), and until they do a share refuses with that instruction rather than falling back to somebody else’s credential. Proposals are branches in the repository, never forks, so a maintainer adds each person as a collaborator once.
A share refused for lack of write access means exactly that, and a collaborator invitation clears it. GitHub answers two other refusals with the same status code, and both are organization policy that no collaborator change and no reconnect touches. An organization behind single sign-on wants the person to authorize the Crystalline app for it, at the address in the message, alone in a browser. An organization that restricts third-party apps needs one of its owners to approve the app under its third-party access settings, and the message says how the person requests that. Each refusal names its page and who has to act, so relay it as written.

An agent reaching the instance over HTTP shares as its user, the account its token belongs to (Chapter 12), so its proposals carry that person’s name like anything else they did. A write it makes records the client in the engram’s provenance as the harness’s name, the word for and the account, so a later reader can tell whose session wrote it. The older arrangement, a bot account named by github.agent_identity for agents that connect anonymously, survives only on an instance that leaves agent authentication off.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
text:
13.3 Review mode

A shared instance has one honest weakness, and chapter 12’s instance walks straight into it: the working tree is what everybody reads. An edit you make at ten is in everybody’s search results at one minute past, reviewed or not, and the proposal that goes to GitHub that afternoon reviews something that already had its effect. For a domain the whole company routes questions to, it’s a gate with no door.

Review mode puts the door back, and the way it does it is a private overlay per person over the shared folder. Every write by every actor, a person in Fluid, an agent acting as that person, the machine’s owner at the terminal, lands in that actor’s own overlay: a layer of changed and added engrams and, for a deletion, a tombstone that hides the file for its author until a merged share removes it for everyone. Underneath, the on-disk folder changes only by pull, so it always equals what the team reviewed and merged. A draft is searchable, readable, routable and editable by the one who wrote it, and invisible to everybody else.

The mode is per domain and it’s deployment choice rather than knowledge, so it lives in the domain’s registration, review: overlay, never in the manifest. crystalline domain review engineering overlay turns it on, or the review card on the domain’s page in Fluid. There’s no tool for it, since an agent doesn’t decide how a team reviews. It needs a GitHub origin, which rules a virtual domain out, and it refuses while the domain holds unshared changes, listing them. Turning it off is the more careful motion, because every actor may hold drafts. The command previews what each person has, and you say per person whether to fold their drafts into the folder or discard them.

In review mode sharing gets simpler, because “my changes” is exact: the share is the actor’s drafts against the reviewed folder, no guessing from who last wrote a file, and scoping selects within them. The drafts stay after the share, since they’re still the working copy, and the merge is what clears them. When the pull brings the folder up to what was merged, every draft that now equals the folder disappears on its own, and a draft the folder moved under in the meantime surfaces as its author’s conflict, nobody else’s. Withdrawing with revert restores content into the overlay it came from, never into the folder.

The privacy of drafts has one deliberate exception, and it’s a number. Everyone sees how many draft changes of their own are waiting, in Fluid and in origin_status. The owner and the instance’s admins also see how many each person holds, never a word of what they say. The operator can still edit the folder on disk, and the domain reports that as edited outside review, naming the paths. And on a solo instance the mode gates nothing between you and your own agent, because the agent acts as you and drafts in your overlay. To review the agent’s work as if it were somebody else’s, give it its own account, which is the rule for a person too.







Figure 13.2: One shared instance in review mode: each actor drafts in a private overlay above the domain folder, a draft goes out as a pull request, and only a merged pull changes the folder.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
text:
13.4 Working on a draft together

A private draft still needs a second pair of eyes before it goes to review, and the answer is a link. In the editor of your own draft, Share draft mints one (the address is /draft/ plus the token). The first signed-in account to open it is the one it binds to, whatever its role. It grants exactly one thing, sight of that one engram in your overlay, nothing of your other drafts and nothing in search, and it’s yours to revoke at any moment. Editing it in the normal editor takes the domain’s write right on top, which the link never adds: a viewer, or a colleague who isn’t a member of a private domain, opens the draft read-only and is told why. Links are the only way one person’s drafts are ever visible to another.
Then the two of you are in one page, and Fluid makes that literal. Open an engram somebody else has open and you see their cursor. Type, and both sets of edits merge conflict-free and land as one save (Chapter 7). That much is pair programming on a document.

The third cursor can be the agent’s. On an instance where agents authenticate, an agent whose session touches an engram its user has open appears in the participant strip as a named peer, the account with an agent designation and a colour of its own. Its edits are computed against the page as it stands that second, so they compose with what somebody typed a moment ago. Its reads see the unsaved text, and its write receipts say the change landed in a live page and name who’s present. The example below puts a meeting in that room.






Figure 13.3: Live co-editing: two cursors in one engram.










NoteIn practice



Your book club has to pick next year’s list, and the argument has run for three meetings. You book an hour and, instead of a poll, open a draft engram in club (in review mode), “Reading list decision”, send Dallas and Kane a draft link each and put the page on the screen. The three of you argue in the page. Your agent is in the strip too, under your name with the agent badge, because you asked it to sit in. When Dallas writes “we did three fantasy doorstops in a row last year and everyone gave up on the third” it pulls up last year’s list and the engram about the third one and drops both into a section headed Prior decisions, with addresses. When Kane asks whether the new Doctorow is even out in paperback by March, the agent reads the publisher’s page while the humans keep talking and adds a paragraph with the answer and a link, in its own colour.
When the hour ends the decision is in the engram, with the options that lost and why, the paperback dates, the prior decisions it leans on and three observations tagged #reading-list. There are no minutes to write, because the whiteboard was the knowledge base. You share it as a proposal before you leave the room, Lambert reviews it on her phone and it merges that evening. When the merged list comes down the draft is gone, and the next morning every agent in the club recalls a decision made and captured in the same hour, the Yavin 4 briefing room with the plan on the screen when they walk out.

title: 13  Sharing with a team
section: 13.5 When two people changed the same file
text:
13.5 When two people changed the same file
Sometimes the team merged a change to an engram you also changed. update_domain brings the merge in, leaves your file untouched rather than guessing, and flags the conflict. origin_status lists its path and kind, and sharing refuses until it’s settled. In Fluid the same conflict opens a dialog with both versions next to each other, so the choice is made with the wording in front of you.

In review mode the conflict belongs to the draft’s author alone, and the resolution is written into their overlay, so nobody else’s view moves until the resolved draft is proposed and merged like anything else.







TipUnder the hood



Settling a conflict is resolve_conflict: mine keeps your version, theirs takes the team’s, merged takes content you supply after reconciling both. On a harness that can ask, calling it without a resolution previews both sides and puts the question to you.
A proposal is a branch in the team’s own repository and never a fork, and stacking is probed once per origin, so a forge that cannot stack falls back without configuration. Overlay drafts are rows in the index with an actor dimension, so search, relations and recency gain the draft view from one condition. Because the index is disposable while drafts aren’t, every draft is also mirrored as plain markdown in a journal under the state directory, from which a wiped and resynced index restores them. The folder itself is written by exactly one thing, the pull.


Review was never the team distrusting a colleague. It was the team trusting a process, and now the colleague can be an agent.







NoteIn brief



A team domain tracks a GitHub repository with no git involved: connect once with a browser code, add the domain with its origin, and five collaboration tools appear. Knowledge goes out with share_changes as a proposal the agent previews and relays but never merges; feedback returns through update_domain, an amend answers on the same proposal, further shares stack and personal identities put each person’s name on their own work. Review mode gives every actor a private overlay over the shared folder: drafts live there, a share is exactly that actor’s drafts, merged pulls clear them, the folder never changes any other way and owners see counts of pending work, never content. A draft is opened to a colleague with a revocable link, edited live with cursors that merge into one save and joined by the agent as a named peer, so a meeting held in an engram is captured when it ends. A conflict is settled with resolve_conflict or Fluid’s side-by-side dialog: mine, theirs or merged.

title: 14  Identity and access
text:
14.1 Who is acting
Every action on a shared instance has a name attached, and the name is a person’s. Chapter 12 ended on that line. This chapter is what follows from taking it seriously: who is acting when an engram changes, who may see a domain and who may change it, how a login at the company’s identity provider becomes an account here, what the rules cover and the few things you do on an ordinary Tuesday. It ends where the whole book has been walking: a colleague who has earned access, by name.
People arrive as accounts, by whichever of chapter 12’s doors they came through. Once inside there’s one account with one role, viewer, editor or admin, and everything the person does is done as it (Chapter 12).
Agents arrive as somebody’s agent. Chapter 12 issued the token, and what it means is the point here. An authenticated agent is its user for the length of the session, with that person’s visibility, that person’s write rights, that person’s share identity in a team domain and that person’s name in the provenance of everything it captures, beside the client that acted. Programs in Tron look like their users and act for them, and that’s the picture: the agent’s name is its user’s name with an agent designation after it. The CLI and a stdio session on the server stay the machine’s owner, as chapter 12 said.
